questions.question: How do you create a custom error type in Go?
questions.title: Custom errors with structured fields
questions.direct_answer: Define a named type, usually a struct, and give it an `Error() string` method so it satisfies the built-in `error` interface. Store fields that callers genuinely need, return the value as `error`, and let callers retrieve the documented type with `errors.As`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Implicit interface satisfaction and deliberate structured error design.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a custom type that carries no useful data or exposing sensitive fields in its message.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a type that supports both a human message and programmatic branching.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A custom type becomes an error by implementing `Error() string`.
Struct fields can carry machine-readable context.
Return it through the `error` interface in most APIs.
Use `errors.As` to retrieve the type through wrappers.
Keep Error methods safe and avoid leaking secrets in their text.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A custom Go error is a named type whose method set includes `Error() string`. A struct is common because it can retain information such as a field name, operation, limit, or underlying cause. The method supplies the readable summary required by the `error` interface.

For example, a validator can return `&ValidationError{Field: "age", Reason: "must be positive"}`. Generic code still handles it as an `error`, while a form layer can use `errors.As` to recover the fields and attach feedback to `age`. The message and the structured contract support different consumers.

I normally return the value through an `error` result rather than changing the function signature to `*ValidationError`. That keeps success represented by a true nil interface and allows future failure kinds. If the error wraps a cause, the type can also implement `Unwrap() error` so standard inspection reaches it.

A custom type is worthwhile only when callers use its identity or data. One class per sentence adds noise. The `Error` method should not panic, should be understandable with useful context, and should avoid credentials or personal data because errors often reach logs. I document any exported type as part of the package's compatibility promise.

sections.title: Design the data before the sentence
sections.content:
Start with the caller's recovery decision. If it must highlight one input, a `Field` member is meaningful. If it must retry after a delay, a typed duration may be meaningful. Fields that no caller reads are usually just duplicated prose.

The display method can combine those fields into a short explanation, but consumers should not reverse that sentence back into data. `errors.As` preserves the type relationship across added context and avoids fragile parsing.

sections.title: One error serves people and programs
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[ValidationError] --> B[Field: age]
  A --> C[Reason: must be positive]
  A --> D[Error method]
  D --> E[Readable log text]
  A --> F[errors.As]
  F --> G[Form highlights age field]
```

questions.question: How does errors.As retrieve a custom error through wrapping?
questions.title: Inspecting custom errors with errors.As
questions.direct_answer: `errors.As(err, &target)` searches the error's unwrap tree for the first value assignable to the target type. When it finds one, it stores that value in the target and returns true. This lets callers read custom fields even after other layers add context with `%w`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Correct target shape, unwrap traversal, and safe use of extracted fields.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a direct type assertion on a wrapped error or passing the wrong target form.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace a custom error through a context wrapper and compare As with an assertion.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Declare a target variable of the concrete error type.
Pass a pointer to that target into `errors.As`.
As searches through `%w` and other `Unwrap` relationships.
Check the returned boolean before reading the target.
A direct type assertion sees only the current outer error.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`errors.As` is used when a caller needs a particular concrete error type and its fields. It examines the outer error and then traverses the unwrap tree. When it finds a value assignable to the requested target type, it assigns that value and reports success.

For example, if a parser returns `*LineError` and a service wraps it as `parse upload: %w`, a direct assertion such as `err.(*LineError)` fails because the visible outer value is the wrapper. Declaring `var lineErr *LineError` and calling `errors.As(err, &lineErr)` succeeds through that layer.

The extra address is important: As needs a place to store the found value. The target must be a non-nil pointer to a type that implements error, or to an interface type; invalid targets panic. Code must also check the boolean before dereferencing the result.

I use As when structured details affect behavior, such as highlighting a line or choosing a retry delay. For a simple yes-or-no category, `errors.Is` and a sentinel are clearer. Both approaches depend on deliberately preserved wrapping. If a package does not promise the concrete type, callers should not couple themselves to an internal implementation.

sections.title: Inspect type without removing context
sections.content:
The caller does not need to unwrap one layer at a time or know how many layers exist. It describes the type it wants, and the standard traversal locates the first compatible node. The original outer error remains intact for logging.

This is especially useful at boundaries: a transport layer can translate a typed domain error while still recording the full contextual message. The extraction is a read of the error tree, not a replacement of it.

sections.title: Type search through context
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[parse upload wrapper] -->|Unwrap| B[LineError]
  C[errors.As target LineError] --> A
  A --> D{assignable?}
  D -- No --> B
  B --> E{assignable?}
  E -- Yes --> F[Set target and return true]
```

questions.question: When should you use a sentinel error instead of a custom error type?
questions.title: Sentinel errors versus custom types
questions.direct_answer: Use a sentinel when callers only need to recognize one stable category, such as not found. Use a custom error type when they need structured details, such as the invalid field and reason. Both are API commitments; choose the smallest contract that supports a real caller decision.

interviewer_intent.testing: Selecting an error contract from the information a caller actually needs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using one custom type for every message or one sentinel for failures that need details.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare the public compatibility cost as well as the code shape.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A sentinel represents one shared yes-or-no category.
A custom type represents a category plus structured fields.
Call sentinels with `errors.Is` and types with `errors.As`.
Wrap either form when added context should preserve inspection.
Do not export error identities that callers cannot use meaningfully.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I choose a sentinel when the caller needs only a stable yes-or-no category. `ErrNotFound` is enough if the useful question is simply whether to return a 404. The package declares one value, returns or wraps it, and callers use `errors.Is`.

I choose a custom type when the caller needs data. For example, validation may need `Field`, `Rule`, and perhaps a safe value description so a UI can place feedback correctly. The caller uses `errors.As` and reads those fields without parsing text.

A custom type can also wrap a cause, and a sentinel can be surrounded by formatted context, so neither choice prevents a useful message. The distinction is the inspection contract: identity alone versus identity plus structured information. A predicate function is another option when the package wants to control classification without exposing a value or type.

Exporting either a sentinel or a type creates compatibility obligations because callers may branch on it. I avoid exposing dependency-specific errors accidentally and translate them into the package's own vocabulary. My default is the smallest stable contract that enables a genuine recovery or presentation decision; ordinary undifferentiated failures can remain plain errors.

sections.title: Let caller questions shape the error model
sections.content:
Error design begins with what code will ask. If the only query is 'was it missing?', one shared marker is sufficient. If the query is 'which field failed and why?', a record with named fields is necessary.

More structure is not automatically better. Every exported identity becomes behavior a package must preserve. Translate private dependency failures into a compact public model so callers receive useful stability rather than accidental implementation details.

sections.title: Pick the public error contract
sections.content:
| Caller needs | Representation | Inspection | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| One category | Sentinel value | `errors.Is` | `ErrNotFound` |
| Named details | Custom type | `errors.As` | `*ValidationError` |
| Only readable context | Plain or formatted error | Display or propagate | `load config failed` |
| Package-controlled classification | Predicate function | Package helper | `os.IsNotExist` style API |
